Dear lavaan group members:

I run the next syntax with my database highlow(uploaded)

highlow[,2]<-as.ordered(highlow[,2])
highlow[,3]<-as.ordered(highlow[,3])
highlow[,4]<-as.ordered(highlow[,4])
highlow[,5]<-as.ordered(highlow[,5])
highlow[,6]<-as.ordered(highlow[,6])
highlow[,7]<-as.ordered(highlow[,7])

TWO.DIM <- "DIM1 =~ v1 + v2 + v3; DIM2 =~ v4 + v5 + v6"

#For lavaan
conffit <- cfa(TWO.DIM, data=highlow, group="condition") #configural
loadfit <- cfa(TWO.DIM, data=highlow, group="condition", group.equal="loadings", parameterization="theta") #loadings
thrfit <- cfa(TWO.DIM, data=highlow, group="condition", group.equal=c("loadings", "thresholds"), parameterization="theta")#loadings+thresholds
resfit <- cfa(TWO.DIM, data=highlow, group="condition", group.equal=c("loadings", "thresholds","residuals"), parameterization="theta") #loadings+thresholds+residuals
meanfit <- cfa(TWO.DIM, data=highlow, group="condition", group.equal=c("loadings", "thresholds","residuals","means"), parameterization="theta")#loadings+thresholds+residuals+means
conffit
loadfit
thrfit
resfit
meanfit

#For semTools
mIC <- measurementInvarianceCat(TWO.DIM, data=highlow, group="condition", strict=T)

fit.loadings   20          56.053      1.332       4  0.8559560

fit.means      56         177.387     14.544       2  0.0006946 ***


There are two differences when I compared both results. First, the results of chisq for loading invariances are very different 63.001 (lavaan) vs 56.053 (semTools). Second, a little difference comparing chisq of configural results 55.033 (lavaan) vs 55.034 (semTools).

I am a bit confused. Are there something that I am doing wrong? There are different models behind the lavaan and semTools commands? 

Best,

Ale

The measurementInvarianceCat() function follows a different pattern of constraints, following the method described in a Millsap & Yu-Tein, as cited on the semTools maintainer's web page:

http://www.sunthud.com/catInvariance.html

Terry

parts:
I also posted a more detailed response when the same original poster opened a new thread on this topic:

https://groups.google.com/d/msg/lavaan/zflFWjOcbjs/aswGeRyrAgAJ
had some evidence for weak invariance.

invariance is the null hypothesis, so you can't have evidence in favor of it, only against it (i.e., reject or fail to reject the null), unless you use Bayesian methods to calculate a Bayes factor with the likelihood of the null in the numerator.

"We further investigated the measurement invariance for gender following Milsap and Yun-Tein(2004). There were no evidence for strict or strong invariance but the test for weak invariance was almost insignificant

There is no "almost" significant in NHST.  Your alpha level, albeit arbitrary, is the boundary used to make a binary decision. You never know whether you've made a Type I error by rejecting (or Type II error by failing to reject) the null, but you can only know your probability of making a Type I error = alpha if you treat the alpha level like it is supposed to be treated.  (I'm not always a proponent of NHST, I'm just pointing out that we should either commit to doing NHST correctly or find another way to answer our research questions, e.g., examining impact of noninvariance on latent parameter estimates to see whether it is even worth worrying about, or using Bayes factors to compare evidence in favor of competing hypotheses).

Terry

The issue is, I get different results using measurementInvarianceCat and

Different than what?  A model you specified yourself?  You can compare your fitted model to the one fitted by measurementInvarianceCat(), e.g., by comparing their parameter tables.

myFit <- cfa(...)
out <- measurementInvarianceCat(...)
autoFit <- out[[1]]
myPT <- parTable(myFit)
autoPT <- parTable(autoFit)
View(myPT)
View(autoPT)
